beats.label: Who
beats.text: I'm Anuvik. I spent nearly 3 years at Oracle as a Software Engineer II on NSX, owning production infrastructure: observability, incident response, and Kubernetes for 37,000+ enterprise tenants.

beats.label: Proof
beats.text: Two results I'm proudest of: I cut P1 MTTR from 94 to 26 minutes by building real-time API diagnostics that auto-tag root causes, so on-call starts with runbook context. And I moved alerting from static thresholds to SLOs, which cut false pages 41%.

beats.label: Pivot
beats.text: I came to USC for my MS to go deep on AI. This summer at MSRcosmos I shipped a multi-agent ERP migration on the Claude API and LangGraph, with a human-in-the-loop layer that auto-approved 83% of records and took turnaround from 3 days to 5.5 hours.

beats.label: Now
beats.text: Today I build a multi-agent app on Claude Enterprise and MCP at USC Annenberg, and I benchmark frontier LLMs for factual accuracy at the AI Trust Lab.

beats.label: Why you
beats.text: Your team is moving Salesforce onto GCP and building AI SRE tooling to cut MTTD and MTTR. I've worked that problem from both sides: as the engineer getting paged, and as the one building agents.

pitch.closing_line: The incident tooling I built by hand at Oracle is what AI SRE agents can automate, on GCP and at Salesforce scale.

template.s: Look in your Oracle deploys before the CLI toolchain existed, or an early MSRcosmos agent run that posted wrong. What broke, and who felt it?
template.t: What were you on the hook for when it broke?
template.a: What did you do in the first hour, and what did you change so it could not happen the same way again?
template.r: The fix, the number if there is one, and the one habit you kept. End on what you do differently now.

template.s: A teammate or another team disagreed with a technical call. Candidates: SLO alerting replacing thresholds, or a team resisting the CLI validation gate.
template.t: What decision was at stake, and who owned it?
template.a: How you understood their position first, what data you brought, and how you reached a decision. Name the compromise if there was one.
template.r: What shipped, how the relationship ended up, and what you learned about disagreeing well.

template.s: Someone newer than you: an engineer onboarding to the CLI toolchain, a new on-call engineer using your runbooks, or a lab teammate.
template.t: What did they need to get to, and by when?
template.a: How you taught it: pairing, docs, reviews. Be specific about one thing you did.
template.r: What they could do on their own afterward. A number if you have one, a concrete outcome if not.

probes.q: Why SLOs instead of tuning thresholds?

p99 latency: 99% of requests are faster than this; it shows the slow tail users feel.

Tenant: one customer organization sharing the platform with others.
stack: Prometheus: collects metrics over time and evaluates alert rules.
Grafana: dashboards that visualize Prometheus data.

simple: Old alerts fired on fixed numbers, so people got paged for nothing.
I defined what good looks like for users: CPU, memory, and p99 latency targets.

terms: CI/CD: automation that tests code on every change (CI) and ships it (CD).
Pre-deployment validation: checks that run before a release to catch mistakes early.
Config error: a wrong setting rather than wrong code; it often breaks production quietly.
Failed deploy rate: the share of releases that break and need a rollback.
stack: Jenkins: the CI/CD server that runs the pipelines.
CLI (command-line tool): one command engineers run locally or in the pipeline.
Validation scripts: rules that check configs before they ship.
simple: Config mistakes kept reaching production; 11% of deploys failed.
I built one command that checks configs before release.
I wired it into Jenkins so every pipeline ran it automatically.
Teams adopted it because it saved them rollbacks: 4 teams in total.
Result: failed deploys from 11% to 4%, release cycles 34% shorter.

stories.title: ModelScope: INT4 at 62% less memory, same accuracy
prompts: Tell me about a performance trade-off you measured.
How would you pick a model for cost and latency?
resume_lines: Benchmarked Llama-3.2-3B and Gemma-2-2B across 8 quantization configs (FP16, INT8, INT4, NF4) on a T4 GPU, profiling inference latency, throughput, and peak memory with PyTorch and CUDA.
Landed INT4 at 2299 MB, 62% below FP16, sustaining 13.7 tok/s with MMLU within a point of baseline; a Pareto sweep ruled INT8 strictly dominated at 53% more memory and 2.1x lower throughput.
stories.s: People pick quantization settings on gut feel. I wanted measured trade-offs on a cheap, common GPU.
stories.t: Benchmark two small models across 8 quantization configs and find which settings are worth using.
a: Ran Llama-3.2-3B and Gemma-2-2B in FP16, INT8, INT4, and NF4 on a T4.
Profiled latency, throughput, and peak memory with PyTorch and CUDA.
Checked quality with MMLU against the FP16 baseline.
Plotted a Pareto sweep to see which configs are never the best choice.
stories.r: INT4 used 2299 MB, 62% below FP16, at 13.7 tok/s with MMLU within a point. INT8 was strictly dominated: 53% more memory and 2.1x lower throughput than INT4.

probes.q: Why was INT8 slower?
probes.a: [fill: your explanation from profiling]. A common cause is INT8 kernels that dequantize at runtime on GPUs without fast INT8 paths.

probes.q: Would you ship INT4?
probes.a: For latency- and cost-bound serving, yes, after checking quality on the real task, not just MMLU.

terms: Quantization: storing model weights with fewer bits to save memory and speed things up.
FP16, INT8, INT4, NF4: 16-bit floats, 8-bit integers, 4-bit integers, and a 4-bit format tuned for model weights.
Throughput (tok/s): tokens generated per second.
MMLU: a standard multiple-choice knowledge test used to check quality loss.
Pareto sweep: find the options where you cannot improve one metric without hurting another.
stack: PyTorch and CUDA: run and profile the models on the GPU.
T4 GPU: a common, low-cost 16 GB inference card.
Llama-3.2-3B and Gemma-2-2B: the two models tested.
simple: I ran 8 quantization settings on two small models.
I measured memory, speed, and accuracy for each.
I plotted the trade-offs to see which settings are never worth it.
Result: INT4 used 62% less memory with almost no accuracy loss; INT8 was slower and bigger than INT4.

stories.title: Graph neural network for fraud: 0.923 ROC-AUC
prompts: Tell me about a model that beat a strong baseline.
How do you handle very imbalanced data?
resume_lines: Constructed a heterogeneous IEEE-CIS fraud graph (726K nodes, 19.5M edges), capturing multi-hop links that flat tabular models miss.
Trained a HeteroRGCN with neighbor sampling and focal loss on a 3.5% fraud rate, reaching 0.923 ROC-AUC, +0.03 over tuned XGBoost.
stories.s: Fraud rings share cards, devices, and emails. Flat tables treat each transaction alone and miss those links.
stories.t: Model the links directly and beat a tuned XGBoost baseline.
a: Built a heterogeneous graph from IEEE-CIS data: 726K nodes, 19.5M edges.
Trained a HeteroRGCN, a GNN that handles several relation types.
Used neighbor sampling so training fits in memory.
Used focal loss because only 3.5% of transactions are fraud.

probes.q: Is +0.03 AUC meaningful?
probes.a: At fraud scale, small ranking gains catch more fraud at the same review budget. [fill: precision at your chosen threshold if you have it]

probes.q: Why focal loss over class weights?
probes.a: Focal loss down-weights easy examples so training focuses on the hard, rare fraud cases.

terms: Graph: nodes (like cards or devices) connected by edges (shared use).
Heterogeneous graph: several node and edge types in one graph.
GNN (graph neural network): learns from a node and its neighbors.
Focal loss: a loss that focuses training on hard, rare cases like fraud.
ROC-AUC: how well the model ranks fraud above normal; 1.0 is perfect, 0.5 is a coin flip.
stack: IEEE-CIS fraud dataset: the public transaction data.
HeteroRGCN: a GNN for graphs with multiple relation types.
Neighbor sampling: train on small subgraphs so a 19.5M-edge graph fits in memory.
XGBoost: the tabular baseline it beat.
simple: Fraudsters share cards, devices, and emails, which flat tables miss.
I built a graph with 726K nodes and 19.5M edges to capture those links.
I trained a GNN with focal loss because only 3.5% is fraud.
Result: 0.923 ROC-AUC, 0.03 better than tuned XGBoost.

values.name: Trust
values.angle: Nothing an agent does should surprise the customer. Confidence routing and SLO-based pages are both about earning trust with evidence.

values.name: Customer Success
values.angle: Measure what the customer feels: page load time, minutes of outage, days waiting for a migration.

values.name: Innovation
values.angle: Use agents where they remove toil, and keep a human on anything irreversible.

values.name: Equality
values.angle: Build tools any engineer can use, not only the most senior: runbook context on every page, one command to validate a deploy.

values.name: Sustainability
values.angle: Spend compute on real demand: autoscale on load, merge incrementally, quantize when quality holds.
